purpose: Attack the frozen E2 rubric for misjudgment using the fitness single-image video as contrast, plus one unmeasurable counter-example.

attack_1_complexity_bias.threat: A rubric that equates 'more shots = better editing' would fail both real videos for being single-image, and would reward a hypothetical 8-image video regardless of whether its images fit the story.
attack_1_complexity_bias.result: NEUTRALIZED. d1 is scored as image-story RELEVANCE, not shot count: Fitness (0/6 scripted scenes, but theme-adjacent image) scores PARTIAL; Love_Hidden (0/8 scripted scenes AND theme-incoherent image) scores FAIL_CANDIDATE. The discriminator is coherence, not complexity.
attack_1_complexity_bias.measured_on: review_fitness_reset.json d1 vs review_love_hidden.json d1 (same rubric, same static-image format, different outcomes)

attack_2_scene_count_as_proxy.threat: A rule that scores 'scripted scenes implemented: 0/8 → auto FAIL' would have failed BOTH videos identically and would have learned nothing the image itself doesn't show.
attack_2_scene_count_as_proxy.result: PARTIALLY ACCEPTED. Scene fidelity IS recorded as factual evidence (0/8, 0/6) but the verdict-driving dimension is d1 relevance. Scene-count alone cannot distinguish Fitness from Love_Hidden; relevance does. However, if the Owner rules multi-scene a hard requirement, scene-count becomes binding at the E3/consumer layer — the rubric deliberately keeps that ruling out of E2.

attack_3_multi_image_wrong_story_hypothe.threat: '8 images, all wrong-theme' counter-example: a rule rewarding image count would score it above both real videos.
attack_3_multi_image_wrong_story_hypothe.result: RECORDED AS ARGUMENT ONLY — NOT MEASURED. Producing such a video would require generating new content, which this trial must not do (no auto re-edit / no new content production). The rubric's d1 wording ('relate to the story the script describes') already excludes it by construction; any future rubric revision must keep a negative control of this class before claiming improvement.

attack_4_e1_to_e2_transfer.threat: Both videos hold E1 technical PASS from round 2 (exact-SHA receipts); a rule letting E1 PASS leak into E2 would auto-PASS both.
attack_4_e1_to_e2_transfer.result: NEUTRALIZED. Rubric anti-gaming rule 4 forbids the transfer; both reviews keep overall_e2 = NOT_PASS despite E1 PASS. This is the round-1 lesson ('exporter status:ok ≠ media verified') extended one layer up.

attack_5_char_speed_auto_fail.threat: A rule that auto-fails any cue above ~20 chars/sec would fail Fitness (cue3: 22.50 cps) on its best-executed short cue and would have failed nothing about Love_Hidden's actual worst problem (130-138 char blocks).
attack_5_char_speed_auto_fail.result: NEUTRALIZED. Char speed is a flagged risk (rubric d3), never an automatic FAIL; verdicts are driven by block density, occlusion and typography, which the speed metric cannot see.
attack_5_char_speed_auto_fail.measured_on: SRT stats: Fitness max 22.50 cps (cue3, clean 1-line render) vs Love_Hidden max 21.43 cps (cue5) — the higher-speed cue renders BETTER than several slower cues

conclusion: The frozen six-dimension rubric survived all measurable attacks without amendment; no rubric revision is proposed this round. The one weakness exposed: the rubric cannot judge what it has no evidence for (audio content d5 stays UNKNOWN, not guessed).
